extracted.intended_audience: researchers, journal editors, and readers interested in research integrity / retractions
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating the integrity and plausibility of experimental data and figures in scientific manuscripts (with emphasis on spectroscopy/image data) to detect fabrication, duplication, or other problems that merit correction or retraction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical plausibility of reported data
rubrics_metrics.description: Data and reported results must be physically plausible; the retraction cites a 'pattern that is unphysical' as a basis for action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If reported measurements or patterns contradict physical expectations (are 'unphysical'), that is a substantive red flag. Editors and reviewers should treat physically implausible results as grounds for further scrutiny and potential retraction if fabrication or error is confirmed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniqueness of noise/signals across spectra or images
rubrics_metrics.description: Retraction notice: 'the XPS spectra shown in figure 3 all exhibit an identical noise pattern that is unphysical and is inconsistent with the different samples being investigated.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identical noise patterns or duplicated features across spectra/images claimed to be from different samples imply manipulation or fabrication. Check figures for duplicated curves, identical noise, or merely re-colored/ re-scaled repeats; such duplication is an anti-pattern indicating misconduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition of data fabrication
rubrics_metrics.description: The publisher found that 'some of the data in this paper appears to have been fabricated.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fabrication is unacceptable and, when established, should lead to retraction. Journals should name fabrication explicitly (rather than using euphemisms) and pursue appropriate corrective action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate editorial response: retraction vs correction
rubrics_metrics.description: Commentary: journals must take a proper stance (as IOP has here); corrections are sometimes used where retraction is warranted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When data fabrication or serious misconduct is demonstrated, the appropriate editorial action is retraction rather than a mere correction. Use clear language in notices to reflect the severity of the problem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer and editor responsibility to detect manipulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Comment: 'It probably should have been caught by the reviewers of the paper or the editor.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Peer reviewers and editors should scrutinize figures and raw data for signs of duplication, identical noise patterns, reused images, and implausible results. As detection tools and community awareness improve, these checks should become standard practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accurate and consistent figure labeling and units
rubrics_metrics.description: Comments note axis/units mislabeling (e.g., mg/ml vs pg/ml) as a source of error that can be sloppy or misleading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Figures must be labeled with correct units and consistent scales. Mislabeling can be honest error but may also mask problems; reviewers should check consistency among text, tables, and figure labels to distinguish sloppiness from misconduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorship accountability and responsiveness during investigations
rubrics_metrics.description: Retraction notice lists authors who 'have agreed' and those the journal 'was unable to contact'; the first author 'declined to sign the notice.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All listed authors should be reachable and accountable for their contributions. Transparent author responses during investigations are expected; evasiveness or claiming authorship only when convenient is an anti-pattern and undermines trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of figure/photo reuse across publications
rubrics_metrics.description: Commenters point out identical figures across multiple papers and ask 'How many photographs have been re-used?'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reusing images/figures across different papers (especially when claimed to represent different experiments/samples) is suspicious and often constitutes misconduct. Check for repeated panels, identical photographs, and duplicated plots across an author's publications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency and precise wording in notices
rubrics_metrics.description: Praise for IOP 'use the correct word, too:
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Retraction and misconduct notices should use precise, transparent language (e.g., explicitly stating 'fabrication' when warranted) rather than euphemisms. Clear wording helps the community understand the nature and seriousness of the issue and prevents minimization.
